body.hook: French is spoken on five continents by more than 300 million people, from Montréal to Dakar to Tahiti. La Francophonie is a whole world connected by one language.

study.title: Le monde francophone
study.question: Where in the world is French spoken?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), founded in 1970, brings together dozens of states and governments that share the French language; Canada, Quebec and New Brunswick are members.
20 March is la Journée internationale de la Francophonie.
French around the world: Europe: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Monaco. Africa: Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Mali, Madagascar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (the country with the largest French-speaking population) and others; French is also widely used in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. Americas: Canada, Haiti, Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana. Indian Ocean and Pacific: La Réunion, Mauritius, French Polynesia, New Caledonia.
Sentences: Au Sénégal, on parle français et wolof. La capitale est Dakar. En Haïti, on parle français et créole haïtien.
Activity: groups each take a continent, colour a world map, and write three sentences for one country: language(s), capital, one fact.
study.source: Summary from public sources, including the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie.

body.objective: Students will be able to explore francophone communities in Alberta.

body.hook: Alberta's francophone story goes back to the fur trade, when French-speaking voyageurs and Métis travelled its rivers. Today there are French schools, newspapers, radio and festivals across the province.

vocabulary.definition: a distinct Indigenous people with French, Cree and other roots

study.title: L'Alberta francophone
study.question: What is the story of francophones in Alberta?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
Fur trade: French-speaking voyageurs paddled canoes across the West for fur-trading companies. Many married into First Nations families, and the Métis Nation emerged with its own culture and its language, Michif, which mixes French and Cree.
Communities: French-Canadian settlers founded or settled communities such as Saint-Albert, Saint-Paul, Bonnyville, Falher, Legal and Plamondon, and Edmonton's Bonnie Doon area.
Organizations and media: the Association canadienne-française de l'Alberta (ACFA), founded in 1926, represents Franco-Albertans. Le Franco is Alberta's French-language newspaper. Radio-Canada broadcasts in French in Alberta.
Schools and rights: section 23 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982) gives French-speaking parents in Alberta the right to have their children educated in French where numbers warrant. Today Alberta has francophone school authorities and many French-immersion programs. The University of Alberta's Campus Saint-Jean offers university programs in French.
Activity: create a timeline with five events in French and English, then answer: Pourquoi les droits linguistiques sont-ils importants ?
study.source: Summary from public sources on Franco-Albertan history.

body.objective: Students will be able to compare a francophone tradition with my own.
body.iCan: I can compare a francophone tradition with my own.
successCriteria: I can describe a francophone tradition in French
I can compare it with a tradition from my own life
I can present the comparison using comparison phrases
body.hook: In spring, families across Quebec head to the cabane à sucre to pour hot maple syrup on snow and roll it onto a stick. Every culture has traditions like this, and comparing them shows how much we share.

study.title: Nos traditions
study.question: How are francophone traditions similar to and different from mine?
study.passage:
Traditions (written for this lesson):
Le temps des sucres: in March and April, in Quebec and eastern Canada, people visit a cabane à sucre to eat pancakes, beans, ham and maple syrup, and make tire sur la neige.
Le réveillon: in Quebec and France, families share a big meal late on Christmas Eve or New Year's Eve; in Quebec, tourtière (meat pie) is a classic.
La Chandeleur: on 2 February in France and Quebec, families make crêpes; some flip them holding a coin for good luck.
Le Carnaval de Québec: winter festival with Bonhomme Carnaval, ice sculptures and canoe races on the St. Lawrence.
Comparison phrases: Les deux traditions… (Both traditions…). Comme chez moi, on mange… (Like at my home, we eat…). Par contre, chez moi… (On the other hand, at my home…). C'est différent parce que…
Task: choose one francophone tradition and one tradition from your family or culture. Make a Venn diagram, then write and present 6–8 sentences comparing them.
study.source: Summary of widely known francophone traditions written for this lesson.
steps: Choose a tradition of your own
discussion: Which francophone tradition interests you most?
What do the traditions have in common?
study.product: Present a 6–8 sentence comparison of a francophone tradition and your own, using comme, par contre and les deux.
